content: Depressive disorders are the most common psychiatric comorbidity in individuals with epilepsy, affecting approximately one-third of this population. This comorbidity significantly reduces quality of life. There is concern that many individuals with epilepsy and depression may not be receiving appropriate treatment for their depressive symptoms. This is due to uncertainty about which antidepressants or drug classes are most effective and concerns about the potential risk of worsening seizures. This review aimed to address these issues and provide evidence to guide clinical practice and future research. It is an updated version of a Cochrane Review originally published in 2014. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of antidepressants in treating depressive symptoms in individuals with epilepsy and depression, as well as to assess the impact of these treatments on seizure recurrence. For this update, a comprehensive search of databases including CRS Web, MEDLINE, SCOPUS, PsycINFO, and ClinicalTrials.gov was conducted in February 2021. The World Health Organization Clinical Trials Registry was also searched in October 2019, but it could not be updated due to inaccessibility. No language restrictions were applied during the search. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospective non-randomized studies of interventions (NRSIs) that investigated the use of antidepressants in children or adults with epilepsy. These studies compared antidepressants to placebo, other antidepressants, psychotherapy, or no treatment for depressive symptoms. The primary outcomes assessed were changes in depression scores, including the proportion of participants with more than a 50% improvement in symptoms, mean differences in depression scores, and the proportion of participants achieving complete remission. Changes in seizure frequency were also evaluated, including mean differences, the proportion of participants experiencing seizure recurrence, and episodes of status epilepticus. Secondary outcomes included study withdrawal rates and reasons for withdrawal, quality of life, cognitive functioning, and adverse events. Two independent reviewers extracted data from each included study, and the data were cross-checked for accuracy. The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane tool for RCTs and the ROBINS-I tool for NRSIs. Binary outcomes were presented as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), while continuous outcomes were presented as standardized mean differences (SMDs) or mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs. The review included 10 studies with a total of 626 participants who had both epilepsy and depression. Four of these studies were RCTs, while six were NRSIs. One RCT was a multi-center study comparing an antidepressant to cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). The other three RCTs were single-center studies comparing antidepressants to active controls, placebo, or no treatment. The NRSIs primarily focused on participants with focal epilepsy who were treated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for depression. One NRSI compared SSRIs to CBT. The risk of bias was rated as low for one RCT, unclear for three RCTs, and serious for all six NRSIs. Due to the heterogeneity of treatment comparisons, no meta-analysis of RCT data could be conducted. The certainty of evidence was judged to be moderate to very low across comparisons, primarily due to limited outcome data from single studies and the high risk of bias in NRSIs, which did not adjust for confounding variables. The proportion of participants experiencing more than a 50% improvement in depressive symptoms ranged from 43% to 82% in RCTs and from 24% to 97% in NRSIs, depending on the antidepressant used. One small RCT (64 participants) provided low-certainty evidence that venlafaxine improved depressive symptoms by more than 50% compared to no treatment (mean difference -7.59, 95% CI -11.52 to -3.66). Results from other comparisons were inconclusive. Two studies comparing SSRIs to CBT also reported inconclusive results regarding the proportion of participants achieving complete remission of depressive symptoms. Data on seizure frequency did not suggest an increased risk of seizures with antidepressants compared to control treatments or baseline. Two studies assessed quality of life, but antidepressants did not appear to improve quality of life compared to control treatments. No studies reported on cognitive functioning. Adverse events were reported in two RCTs and one NRSI, and antidepressants did not appear to increase the severity or number of adverse events compared to controls. However, NRSIs reported higher rates of study withdrawals due to adverse events than due to lack of efficacy. Reported adverse events associated with antidepressants included nausea, dizziness, sedation, headache, gastrointestinal disturbances, insomnia, and sexual dysfunction. The authors concluded that the existing evidence on the effectiveness of antidepressants for treating depressive symptoms in individuals with epilepsy is very limited. Response rates to antidepressants were highly variable. Low-certainty evidence from one small RCT suggests that venlafaxine may improve depressive symptoms more than no treatment, but this evidence is limited to short-term treatment (8 to 16 weeks) and does not provide information on long-term effects. Moderate to low-certainty evidence suggests that SSRIs do not increase or exacerbate seizures. However, there is no comparative data available to guide the choice of specific antidepressants or drug classes for efficacy or safety in this population. The authors emphasized the need for future RCTs involving antidepressants from drug classes other than SSRIs, conducted in large samples of individuals with epilepsy and depression. These studies should assess treatment effects over longer durations to account for delayed onset of action, sustainability of treatment responses, and the impact on seizure control.
